sections.h2: Who sends a Hendersonville property tax bill
sections.html:
A house inside Hendersonville is taxed twice, by Sumner County and by the City of Hendersonville, and the two bills come from different offices. The Sumner County Trustee collects the county share, and the city's finance office collects the city share. The Sumner County Assessor of Property sets the value both bills use.

Hendersonville is the largest city in Sumner County, on Old Hickory Lake about 18 miles northeast of Nashville. City hall is at 101 Maple Drive N, Hendersonville, TN 37075. Over in Gallatin, the Trustee works from 355 North Belvedere Drive, Room 107, at (615) 452-1260, weekdays eight to four-thirty. The Assessor can be reached at (615) 452-2412.

The city's Tax Structure page lists a Hendersonville rate of $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value and a Sumner County rate of $1.4210 per $100. Together that is $2.0093 per $100 of assessed value. Homes and farms are assessed at 25% of appraised value. The ratios are 40% for commercial and industrial property and 30% for personal property equipment.

The Board of Mayor and Aldermen approves the city budget each year in a process of about three months, with two readings and a public hearing before it takes effect. That hearing is where a change in the city rate would surface. Budgets can move these rates, so confirm the numbers on your own bill with the finance office and the Trustee.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The city accepts payment starting the first Monday in October, with a due date of the last day of February. Interest of 1.5% a month starts March 1. The county bill follows the same February deadline, and Sumner County adds interest from March 1 as well.

Ways to pay a Hendersonville or Sumner County tax bill
BillPayment methodDetails
CityMailCheck payable to the City of Hendersonville, sent to 101 Maple Drive N; postmark date counts
CityIn personCounter service at City Hall for cash, check, money order or card, plus an always-open dropbox on the front portico for checks and money orders
CityOnlineCity payment portal; cards add a 2.95% convenience fee and an e-check carries a $2.95 fee
CountyOnline, mail, phone or in persontnpayments.com, mail with the notice's top portion, phone, Room 107, or banks named on the back of the notice; card payments cost 2.65% plus $1

The Trustee takes up to five partial payments by check or cash. Any unpaid portion starts collecting interest on March 1.

Because two separate offices send two separate bills, make a habit of checking both. A paid city bill does not clear the county bill, and the reverse is also true. Keep both receipts with your closing papers, and note that the county's online link can show proof of paid taxes for a prior year.

Begin with an informal review by calling the Sumner County Assessor at (615) 452-2412. If that fails, go to the Sumner County Board of Equalization and after that the State Board of Equalization. Informal reviews run in May and the county board convenes June 1 each year. Book your county board appointment well before the deadline, and call the assessor's office to learn the exact date for the current cycle. Sumner's last countywide reappraisal notices went out in 2024.

The assessor lists the kinds of evidence it accepts for homes:

  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Recent photographs.
  • Insurance replacement value or a recent appraisal.
  • Costs to build, and the cost to cure any physical or functional problem.
  • Changes in the physical characteristics of the property.

Gather your proof before you call: comparable sales, recent photographs and any appraisal or insurance replacement figure you have. If the house had storm repairs or physical problems, a cost-to-cure estimate helps show why the value should drop. Keep copies of everything you submit.

Sumner County's Trustee runs the state relief program for elderly, disabled and disabled military service member homeowners, and also a tax freeze program for the county and part of the county's cities. Ask the Trustee whether the freeze covers your Hendersonville address, because the county describes it as covering only a portion of the cities.

Relief for people 65 and older and for disabled homeowners is income based. Relief for totally and permanently disabled military service members, and for their surviving spouses, is not. Applications open when bills are mailed and must be complete within 35 days after the February payment deadline. Freeze applications open in September, and annual requalification is required. To book a phone or online appointment, call (615) 452-1260.

Relief is a payment toward the tax, not an exemption, so you still receive and must pay your bills. It applies to a primary residence only.

The city bill and the county bill both stay attached to the parcel, so your closing agent should request a payoff from each office. Sumner County shows verification of paid taxes under the online payment link, which helps confirm that a prior year is clear.

The Assessor's office handles mailing address changes for county bills, so call (615) 452-2412 after closing so notices reach the new owner. Questions about tax sales in Sumner County go to the Clerk and Master's office.

The Sumner County Register of Deeds records deeds and runs its own records site. Under state rules the grantee, meaning the buyer, pays the transfer tax.

Behind on either bill? Request payoffs from both offices before choosing a closing date, and let the title company know so proceeds can cover them.

Before you list, collect the current balances, your last two bills and the parcel details from the assessor. A buyer's agent will often ask for them early, and having them ready keeps a contract from stalling at the payoff stage. A cash buyer needs the same payoffs, but there is no lender timeline to wait on.

The 2020 census counted 61,753 residents in Hendersonville, and the 2025 estimate is about 64,266, which ranks tenth among Tennessee cities. The city has 25,255 households, and owners occupy 71.7% of homes. Home values center on $430,700, with median rent at $1,653 and median household income at $97,200.

State Route 386 and U.S. 31E carry most traffic. A tornado struck the city on December 9, 2023, so ask for permit records on any house that had storm repairs. The city is governed by a mayor and twelve aldermen.

faqs.q: Does Hendersonville have its own property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The city levies $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value on top of the Sumner County rate of $1.4210. The city collects its own bill at 101 Maple Drive N, and the county Trustee collects the county bill in Gallatin.

faqs.q: When are Hendersonville property taxes due?
faqs.a: Payment is due by the end of February, and you can start paying the first Monday in October. March 1 brings interest at 1.5% a month. Mailed payments count on the postmark date.

faqs.q: How can I pay Hendersonville property tax online?
faqs.a: Use the online payment portal linked from the city's Tax Structure page. Cards carry a 2.95% convenience fee and e-checks a $2.95 processing fee, and both fees may change.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Hendersonville assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Sumner County Assessor at (615) 452-2412 for an informal review in May. The county Board of Equalization opens June 1, with the State Board of Equalization after that.

faqs.q: Who do I call about senior tax relief in Hendersonville?
faqs.a: Call the Sumner County Trustee at (615) 452-1260. Applications are accepted when bills are mailed and until 35 days after the February deadline, and the office books appointments by phone or online.
